message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"1.5","text":"What, then, must I do but this? I will travel to Egypt, befriend the hierophants and prophets of the inner sanctuaries, and, after searching for and finding a magician, persuade him with a great deal of money to summon up a soul—the practice called necromancy—while I inquire as though about some particular matter. But my inquiry will be about learning whether the soul is immortal. I will know the soul’s answer, that it is immortal, not from its speaking or even from my hearing it, but from its merely being seen, so that, after seeing it with my own eyes, I may possess a self-sufficient and adequate verdict, from its mere appearance, that it exists. Then the obscure words belonging to hearing will no longer be able to overturn what belongs peculiarly to the eyes. Nevertheless, I put this very consideration before a philosopher of my acquaintance, who advised me on many grounds not to dare such a thing. “For if the soul does not heed the magician,” he said, “you will live with a guilty conscience because you acted against the laws that forbid people to do these things. But if it does heed him, then, besides your living with a guilty conscience, I think that the concerns of piety will no longer prosper for you, though it was for this very purpose that you dared it. For they say that the divine is hostile to those who harass souls when dead bodies are dissolved.” When I heard this, I became more hesitant to attempt such a thing, but I did not abandon the plan I had formed from the beginning. Rather, as one whose impulse had been obstructed, I was disheartened.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἀναπομπὴν (τὴν λεγομένην νεκρομαντείαν)","chosen":"summon up a soul—the practice called necromancy","rationale":"ἀναπομπή denotes a sending or bringing upward; “summon up” conveys the contextual necromantic sense while retaining that movement."},{"source_quote":"αὐτάρκη καὶ ἱκανὴν ἀπόφασιν","chosen":"a self-sufficient and adequate verdict","rationale":"Retains both coordinated adjectives and presents ἀπόφασις as a settled determination."},{"source_quote":"τὰ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἴδια","chosen":"what belongs peculiarly to the eyes","rationale":"Preserves the contrast between the eyes’ own evidence and the obscure verbal evidence of hearing."},{"source_quote":"δυσσυνειδήτως βιώσεις","chosen":"you will live with a guilty conscience","rationale":"The adverb describes living under an adversely burdened conscience."},{"source_quote":"τῇ λύσει θανόντων σωμάτων","chosen":"when dead bodies are dissolved","rationale":"λύσις denotes loosening or dissolution; the rendering preserves its association with bodily death without specifying a further anthropology."},{"source_quote":"ὀκνηρότερος","chosen":"more hesitant","rationale":"In context the comparative indicates increased reluctance to undertake the proposed act."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"1.6","text":"And, so that I may not recount such things to you at great length, while I was amid so many thoughts and affairs, a certain report, taking its beginning from the spring equinox during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, kept growing gradually and, truly a good messenger of God, ran throughout the world, unable to keep God’s will concealed in silence. Thus it continually became more widespread and greater, reporting that a certain man in Judea, after beginning at the spring equinox, was announcing the eternal God’s kingdom as good news to the Jews, which he said any one of them would enjoy if he first set his way of life right. And, so that it might be believed of him that, being full of divinity, he does these things, he performs many marvelous signs and wonders by command alone, as one who has received the authority from God. For he makes the deaf hear and the blind regain their sight; he makes people with deformed limbs walk and sets the lame upright; he drives away every disease and puts every demon to flight. Even people with leprosy and people with scabby skin conditions, merely gazing intently at him from a distance, depart healed. The dead are raised when brought to him, and there is nothing that he is unable to do. Indeed, the more time advanced, the truth of the matter—not now the report, I mean—became far greater and more firmly established through increasing numbers of visitors. For by then gatherings were even being held in various places for deliberation and inquiry into who the one who had appeared might be and what he intended to say.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"φήμη τις ἠρέμα ἐπὶ τῆς Τιβερίου Καίσαρος βασιλείας ἐξ ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς τὴν ἀρχὴν λαμβάνουσα ηὔξανεν ἑκάστοτε","chosen":"a certain report, taking its beginning from the spring equinox during the reign of Tiberius Caesar, kept growing gradually","rationale":"“Gradually” associates ἠρέμα with the report’s growth, while “kept growing” represents the recurrent force of ἑκάστοτε."},{"source_quote":"ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀγαθὴ θεοῦ ἄγγελος","chosen":"truly a good messenger of God","rationale":"Takes ὡς ἀληθῶς idiomatically as “truly” and preserves the report’s personification as a messenger without identifying it as a celestial being."},{"source_quote":"Ἰουδαίοις τὴν. τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ εὐαγγελίζεται βασιλείαν","chosen":"was announcing the eternal God’s kingdom as good news to the Jews","rationale":"Expresses the good-news force of εὐαγγελίζεται while preserving its object, the kingdom."},{"source_quote":"προκατορθώσῃ τὴν πολιτείαν","chosen":"first set his way of life right","rationale":"προκατορθόω conveys prior rectification, while πολιτεία here concerns conduct or manner of life."},{"source_quote":"θειότητος γέμων","chosen":"full of divinity","rationale":"Preserves the abstract noun θειότης and the image of being filled with it without inferring a contrast from a different Greek noun."},{"source_quote":"κυλλοὺς ποιεῖ περιπατεῖν, χωλοὺς ἀνορθοῖ","chosen":"he makes people with deformed limbs walk and sets the lame upright","rationale":"Uses distinct descriptions for κυλλοί and χωλοί rather than collapsing the two clauses."},{"source_quote":"λεπροὶ ψωροὶ","chosen":"people with leprosy and people with scabby skin conditions","rationale":"Uses a broad description for ψωροί rather than a specific medical diagnosis. The asyndetic phrase may list two groups, as rendered, or describe one group of scabby lepers."},{"source_quote":"συστήματα κατὰ τόπους","chosen":"gatherings were even being held in various places","rationale":"σύστημα denotes an organized gathering or assembly, and κατὰ τόπους distributes the gatherings across locations."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"τὴν. τοῦ ἀιδίου θεοῦ","issue":"The printed full stop interrupts a syntactically continuous article, genitive phrase, and noun. The translation provisionally treats it as editorial punctuation rather than a sentence boundary or evidence of textual corruption.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"1.7","text":"Then, at one point in that same year, at the autumn equinox, someone stood in public and cried out, saying, “Men of Rome, listen! The Son of God is present in Judea, promising eternal life to all who desire it, if they live in accordance with the will of the Father who sent him. Therefore change your way of life, from worse things to better, from temporary things to eternal. Know that there is one God, the heavenly one, whose world you inhabit unjustly before his righteous eyes. But if you change and live according to his will, then, after being carried into another age and becoming everlasting, you will enjoy his unutterable good things. If, however, you disobey, your souls, after the dissolution of the body, will be cast into the place of fire, where, being punished everlastingly, they will reorient themselves to no avail. For each person’s present life is the time for reorientation.” When I heard these things, I was distressed that no one from among so many crowds, after hearing so momentous an announcement, had said, “I will travel to Judea so that I may see whether this man is telling the truth in saying these things—namely, that the Son of God has come to Judea, revealing the will of the Father who sent him for the sake of a good and eternal hope—especially since what they say he proclaims is no small matter. For he firmly assures that the souls of some, being eternal, will enjoy eternal good things, but that those of others, after being cast into unquenchable fire, will be punished forever.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἄνδρες Ῥωμαῖοι, ἀκούσατε","chosen":"Men of Rome, listen!","rationale":"Preserves both the explicit address to men and its Roman civic designation."},{"source_quote":"ἐν φθινοπωρινῇ τροπῇ","chosen":"at the autumn equinox","rationale":"As with the preceding spring τροπή, the seasonal turning point is understood as the equinox."},{"source_quote":"μεταβάλλεσθε τὸν τρόπον","chosen":"change your way of life","rationale":"The verb is μεταβάλλω, not μετανοέω, and τὸν τρόπον identifies the manner or way of life to be changed."},{"source_quote":"ἀπὸ τῶν προσκαίρων ἐπὶ τὰ αἰώνια","chosen":"from temporary things to eternal","rationale":"Preserves the substantival contrast between what lasts only for a time and what is eternal."},{"source_quote":"τῶν ἀπορρήτων αὐτοῦ ἀγαθῶν","chosen":"his unutterable good things","rationale":"“Unutterable” leaves open whether ἀπόρρητα means things not to be divulged, secret or undisclosed things, or things that cannot be expressed."},{"source_quote":"ἀνωφέλητα μετανοήσουσιν","chosen":"they will reorient themselves to no avail","rationale":"Renders μετανοέω with the supplied terminology while preserving the explicit claim that this postmortem reorientation is ineffective."},{"source_quote":"ὁ γὰρ τῆς μετανοίας καιρὸς","chosen":"the time for reorientation","rationale":"Uses the corresponding rendering for μετάνοια without adding a destination absent from the Greek."},{"source_quote":"τὸν αἰῶνα κολασθήσεσθαι","chosen":"will be punished forever","rationale":"The accusative temporal expression presents the punishment as continuing through the age, idiomatically rendered here as “forever.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"σώματος·λύσιν","issue":"The printed medial stop falls within the syntactically continuous phrase consisting of the dependent genitive σώματος and λύσιν. The translation treats the punctuation provisionally as non-boundary punctuation, without alleging textual corruption.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὡς ὅτι υἱὸς θεοῦ ἐπιδεδήμηκεν τῇ Ἰουδαίᾳ","issue":"The discourse force of ὡς ὅτι and the scope of the preceding imagined quotation remain uncertain. The translation provisionally takes the clause as specifying the reported content—“namely, that”—and continues the imagined speaker’s words through the following explanation. Alternatively, the clause may stand outside the quotation as the narrator’s explanatory assertion. The supplied wording is retained, and no textual corruption is established.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]},{"reference":"1.8","text":"As I said these things about others, I also addressed myself, saying, “Why do I blame others when I am under the same charge of negligence? No, I will set out for Judea, after first putting my life in order.” Yet, after I had resolved on this course, a long period of delay followed, because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from. At last, then, after reflecting somehow on the nature of life—that it lies in ambush for those who hurry, entangling them with hope—and also on the time during which I had once been beguiled, tossed about by hopes, and on the fact that, while occupied in this way, we human beings die, I left all my things just as they were and set out for Portus. After reaching the harbor and putting out to sea, I was carried by the hostility of the winds to Alexandria instead of Judea. Then, detained there by a lack of winds, I associated with the philosophers and related the accounts concerning the report and the man who had appeared in Rome. They answered, “We do not know the man who appeared in Rome. But about the one who appeared in Judea and was called the Son of God by the report, we have heard from many who had come from there too, and we have learned about all the wonders he performed as he spoke.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"πρότερον τὸν ἐμὸν διαθεὶς βίον","chosen":"after first putting my life in order","rationale":"διατίθημι here indicates arranging or settling one’s life and affairs before departure."},{"source_quote":"τῶν βιωτικῶν πραγμάτων δυσεκλύτων ὄντων","chosen":"because the affairs of life were difficult to break free from","rationale":"Preserves both the practical affairs denoted by βιωτικά and the difficulty of disengagement expressed by δυσεκλύτων."},{"source_quote":"ἐλπίδι ἐμπλέκων τοὺς σπεύδοντας ἐνεδρεύει","chosen":"it lies in ambush for those who hurry, entangling them with hope","rationale":"Makes ἐλπίδι the means or circumstance of entanglement, while leaving the eagerness or haste of τοὺς σπεύδοντας unspecified."},{"source_quote":"ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος","chosen":"the time during which I had once been beguiled, tossed about by hopes","rationale":"Takes ποτε temporally as “once” and avoids adding a quantitative “how much.” “Beguiled” remains provisional because the construction and force of εἰσεκλάπην are difficult."},{"source_quote":"τὰ πάντα μου ὡς ἔτυχεν ἀφεὶς","chosen":"I left all my things just as they were","rationale":"Preserves the sense that Clement departed without first bringing his possessions or affairs into an orderly condition."},{"source_quote":"εἰς Πόρτον","chosen":"for Portus","rationale":"Πόρτος is treated as the proper name of the port settlement rather than translated generically."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἔχθραις","chosen":"by the hostility of the winds","rationale":"Retains the source’s personifying image rather than reducing it to adverse weather."},{"source_quote":"ἀνέμων ἀπορίᾳ","chosen":"by a lack of winds","rationale":"ἀπορία here indicates a deficiency or absence of wind that prevents onward sailing."},{"source_quote":"περὶ πάντων ὧν λαλῶν ἐποίει θαυμασίων","chosen":"about all the wonders he performed as he spoke","rationale":"The participle may describe wonders performed while speaking or by means of speech; “as he spoke” leaves the precise relation open."}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ. ὃν ποτε","issue":"The printed full stop interrupts the correlative expression οὐ μὴν ἀλλὰ καί and separates it from the additional object of reflection. The translation provisionally reads the syntax continuously while retaining the supplied wording and treating the stop as an editorial feature rather than demonstrated corruption.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":false},{"source_quote":"ὃν ποτε εἰσεκλάπην χρόνον ἐλπίσιν δονούμενος","issue":"The construction remains semantically difficult, especially the force of εἰσεκλάπην with the accusative χρόνον. The translation provisionally understands Clement as having been beguiled or drawn in during that time while hopes tossed him about. The unfamiliar grammar is not classified as a transcription error, and no alteration of the supplied Greek is proposed.","proposed_reading":"","blocks_publication":true}]}]}
